amendments.why: Rule 18's closing sentence marks a supplied possessive with no suffix `added`, and rule 44 itself leaves the possessive of `הָלַךְ` → *go your way* `added` with its supplied object; nothing in the contract says that the possessive of *hold his peace* — a complement that is the verb's own rendering — stays inside the verb's unit. JOB.13 writes the idiom three times (13.5, 13.13, 13.19), and the corpus reads every one of חָרֵשׁ's 42 units as a single unit headed on *peace* with the possessive inside (*hold thy peace* ×7, *held his peace*, *hold his peace*, *holdeth his peace*, *held their peace*, *hold my peace*, etc.), marking none `added`. The amendment states the boundary between the two cases by the subtraction test the rule already runs.
amendments.rule: **A verb the ASV renders as a light verb plus a complement heads on the complement, not on the light verb.** This is rule 31's test applied to a verb: drop each word in turn, and the head is the one whose loss loses the lexeme. `הַאֲזִין` → *Give ear unto* heads on *ear*, because *give* alone gives anything; so too `הִשְׁתַּחֲוָה` → *did obeisance*, `נוֹעַץ` → *took counsel*, `הִמְלִיךְ` → *make king*, `הוֹדָה` → *give thanks*, `כִּלָּה` → *made an end*, `עוּד` → *bear witness*, `חָנַן` → *make supplication*, `בּוֹשׁ` → *put to shame*. The complement need not be a noun: an adjective (`הִכְבִּיד` → *made heavy*, `גָּדַל` → *make greater*) and a second verb (`חָטָא` hiphil → *made to sin*, `אָכַל` → *did eat*) are read the same way. Rule 24's *lexical predicate over subjects and auxiliaries* is about `was gathered`, and must not be read as a preference for the English verb — that reasoning would head *make king* on *make*. **A determiner or possessive the English idiom writes on such a complement is part of that one rendering.** Where the complement carries the source verb's lexeme and English writes it with an article or a possessive the idiom requires — `הֶחֱרִישׁ` → *held his peace*, `כִּלָּה` → *made an end*, `גָּוַע` → *give up the ghost* — that word joins the verb's unit with the complement, is never `added`, and does not move the head, which stays on the complement. Rule 18's closing sentence does not reach it: what that sentence marks `added` is a possessive standing on a noun the Hebrew writes with no suffix, or on a supplied object noun the sentences below leave `added` — `הָלַךְ` → *go* ***your way*** — and a possessive inside a complement that is itself the verb's rendering is neither. Test by subtraction as rule 31 does: drop the complement and the possessive has nothing to stand on, so the two go together, whereas dropping *your way* leaves *go* whole. The corpus reads `חָרֵשׁ` hiphil as *hold thy peace*, *held his peace*, *held their peace* and *hold my peace* in one unit headed on *peace* throughout its forty-two units and marks the possessive `added` in none. **A phrasal particle is not a complement.** `שָׁלַח` → *put forth*, `סוּר` → *take away*, and `נָתַן` → *put away* are one lexical verb plus its particle, and the head stays on the verb; the same subtraction says so, since *forth* and *away* alone name nothing. **But run that same subtraction on the particle before folding it in.** Where the bare English verb already writes the source verb's whole lexeme **and** the particle adds a direction, a result or a repetition the Hebrew does not write, no morpheme licenses that word: it is its own `added` unit under rule 30 and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside its rendering, exactly as this rule leaves a supplied object noun `added` and rule 17 a supplied lexical subject noun. `שׁוּב` → *turn ... again* keeps its *again* with the verb, discontinuous under rule 25, because *turn* alone does not write the returning, and `כָּנַס` → *gather ... together* and `מָצָא` → *find out* keep theirs on the same ground; but `בּוֹא` hiphil → *bring him* ***back*** leaves the *back* `added`, because the hiphil is the bringing and *bring* has already written it. **Both conditions must hold, and the second is read against the whole Hebrew clause and not against the verb alone.** What marks a particle surplus is that it states something the Hebrew has nowhere written, as the return of *bring him back* is: the particles this rule keeps — *out*, *together*, *away*, *forth* — stand beside verbs whose bare English word writes the lexeme quite as plainly as *bring* writes the bringing, so the first condition cannot decide a particle by itself. Where the direction the particle states is written in the clause by a preposition, an adverb or another morpheme, the particle restates what the Hebrew has written rather than supplying what it has not, and it is part of the English phrasal verb by which the ASV renders that verb: it joins the verb's unit, discontinuous around an object under rule 25, and the head is unaffected. `הָלַךְ` with `מִן` → *went* ***away*** *from him* and `לָקַח` with `עַל` → *took her* ***up*** *upon the ass* both keep their particle with the verb, on the same footing as `מָצָא` → *find out*. That the other morpheme holds an English word of its own is not a reason to mark the particle `added`, and it is not an invitation to move the particle onto that morpheme either: the word belongs to the verb's rendering, and a preposition already holding its own English is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw. Read the source verb's lexeme against the bare English verb rather than the shape of the English verb phrase, since the particle of *put forth* and *take away* is what completes a lexeme neither *put* nor *take* writes, and do not fold a surplus particle into the verb, the object or a preposition standing beside it, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and* and rule 51 about a supplied *also*. An ASV italic on such a particle corroborates it and decides nothing, by rule 7. **A supplied object is not a complement either, and that holds of any verb's rendering and not only a light verb's.** Where the ASV writes an object pronoun inside or beside a Hebrew verb's rendering — `וַיַּפֵּל` → *he let* ***it*** *fall*, `וַיַּשְׁקְ` → *gave* ***them*** *drink*, `אֲנִי שָׁמָעְתִּי` → *I have heard* ***it*** — read whether an object morpheme is present. Where one is, it takes the pronoun under rule 18 and the verb keeps the rest, as in `וַיַּעֲבִירֵם` → *caused* ***them*** *to pass through*. Where none is, the pronoun answers to no morpheme, is its own `added` unit under rule 30, and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside or beside its rendering; rule 17's permission reaches a pronoun realizing the verb's own person and number, and never an object the Hebrew does not write, exactly as that rule leaves a supplied lexical subject noun `added`. The verb's unit is discontinuous around such a pronoun under rule 25. **This applies only to a pronoun that truly supplies an object.** A reflexive pronoun the ASV uses to render the Hebrew verb's own voice or its elative sense is part of that verb's unit, because the source verb licenses it: `אִכַּף` → *bow myself* keeps *myself* with the Niphal verb and heads on *bow*, and `הִגְדִּיל עַל` → *magnified yourselves against* keeps *yourselves* with the Hiphil on the same ground. Position inside the English verb phrase is not what makes a word part of the verb's rendering — the complement, or the source verb's own voice or sense, must license it, and an unsupported object does not. **And a pronoun realizing the source verb's own person and number is not a supplied object either, whatever case the English recasting puts it in.** Where the ASV recasts a finite verb impersonally — writing a dummy or anticipatory *it* as the English subject and demoting the verb's own subject to the English object — both words belong to that verb's unit, headed on the lexical verb, exactly as rule 17 keeps a presentative dummy with the finite verb it recasts and rule 21 keeps *it was* with `הָיָה`: `נִלְאָה לַהֲשִׁיבָהּ אֶל־פִּיו` → ***It wearieth him*** *to bring it again to his mouth* gives *It wearieth him* to `נִלְאָה`, while the infinitive and the preposition keep their own English. What the preceding sentences govern is a pronoun denoting a participant the Hebrew never wrote, as the *it* of `וַיַּפֵּל` → *he let it fall* and the *them* of `וַיַּשְׁקְ` → *gave them drink* are; a pronoun denoting the very participant the verb's own person and number denote is not that, and marking it `added` would leave the verb's subject unrendered against rule 2 while an English word plainly realizing it stood unaligned. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the English pronoun and ask whether a participant the Hebrew wrote has lost its rendering, or only one the ASV supplied. Read whom the pronoun denotes rather than the case English puts it in, and read the Hebrew clause before reaching for this sentence: where an object morpheme stands in the clause it takes the pronoun under rule 18 as before, where the ASV writes the verb's subject as an English subject this sentence does not arise, and rule 20's ruling that a cleft or impersonal *it* is `added` governs a verbless clause, where no verb stands to be recast. **A supplied object noun is read on those same terms, and what decides it is whether the English noun writes the verb's own lexeme.** Where the ASV completes a Hebrew verb with an object noun the Hebrew does not write, run rule 31's subtraction on that noun. Where it does not carry the verb's lexeme, it answers to no morpheme, is its own `added` unit under rule 30, and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside its rendering: `לֹא שָׁאָלוּ` → *asked* ***counsel*** *not* leaves *counsel* `added`, because `שָׁאַל` is the asking and *asked* has already written it, and `הָלַךְ` → *go* ***your way*** leaves the supplied noun and its possessive `added` on the same ground, because *go* has written the going and *way* names a path the Hebrew does not write, exactly as rule 17 leaves a supplied lexical subject noun `added` and rule 20 a supplied lexical verb. A supplied noun is not a particle, and the clause-level reading above does not reach it: what that reading keeps with the verb is a word stating a relation the clause writes, and a noun naming a thing the clause never names is not that. Where the noun does carry the lexeme, it is part of that verb's one rendering, joins its unit, and the head goes by the same subtraction to whichever word carries the lexeme: `וַיַּעֲשׂוּ` → *did work* is one unit on the verb, headed on *did*, because `עָשָׂה` is the doing and the working alike and neither English word is a complement the other lacks. Read the source verb's lexeme rather than the English phrase's shape, since this rule's light-verb clause governs where the supplied noun is what carries that lexeme — `נוֹעַץ` → *took counsel* heads on *counsel* — and this sentence governs where the verb's own English word has written it already. A supplied possessive standing on such a noun is disposed of by rule 18's closing sentence and is not made the verb's by the noun beside it. **But a preposition the ASV supplies to reach the verb's own object is part of that rendering.** Where the Hebrew writes a bare direct object — no object marker on it and no preposition of its own — and the English verb reaches that object through a preposition the ASV has written, the preposition belongs to the verb's unit and not to the object noun's: `חָמְסוּ תוֹרָתִי` → *have done violence* ***to*** *my law*, `תְּבַצְּעִי רֵעַיִךְ` → *hast greedily gained* ***of*** *thy neighbors*, `הֵקַלּוּ אָב וָאֵם` → *have set light* ***by*** *father and mother*, `אֲבַקֵּשׁ אִישׁ` → *sought* ***for*** *a man*, `טָחוּ תָּפֵל` → *have daubed ... with untempered mortar*. This is rule 16's reasoning where no marker stands to take the word: the same subtraction test finds that dropping it diminishes nothing but the object relation, and the object noun's own English is the noun. The unit is discontinuous under rule 25 where other material stands between the verb and the preposition, and the head is unaffected — it stays on the lexical verb, or on the complement where this rule's light-verb clause puts it. **And the object so reached may be a pronominal suffix on the verb rather than a noun.** Where a verbal object suffix stands with no preposition of its own and the English rendering reaches it through a supplied preposition — `יִבְּמָהּ` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *her*, `יַבְּמִי` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *me* — that preposition belongs to the verb's unit on exactly the terms just given, and the suffix keeps only the pronoun rule 18 writes for it. Do not read rule 18's *the English pronoun that realizes it* as reaching the preposition standing beside that pronoun: what that rule places is the pronoun, and a preposition the English verb's valency licenses is the verb's whether its object is a noun or a suffix. Rule 40 does not reach such a suffix either, since no preposition morpheme stands in the clause for the recasting to silence. Test by subtraction as before — drop the English preposition and ask whether anything but the object relation is diminished. Two limits. Where an object marker or a preposition of the object's own is present, that morpheme takes the word under rules 16 and 11, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does. And this does not touch rule 33: a function word supplied for an adverbial accusative is licensed by that noun's own case-function and stays with the noun, whereas a word supplied for a direct object is licensed by the English verb's valency, so read which the Hebrew noun is before placing it.

conventions: נָשָׂא פָּנִים → 'show partiality' (13.8, 13.10) is one noncompositional unit on פָּנֶה + the verb: the idiom is rendered by words of its own writing neither lexeme, so the source head is the first token פָּנֶה under rule 6's fallback (the governing verb is the competing head) and the target head is 'partiality' by rule 44's subtraction. The verb's subject pronoun and auxiliary join the unit, as does the 'to' the English verb needs to reach a suffix's 'him' (rule 44); the suffix keeps its own pronoun.

חָרֵשׁ hiphil → 'hold your peace' / 'hold my peace' (13.5, 13.13, 13.19) is one unit headed on 'peace' (rule 44); the possessive the English idiom writes on the complement stays inside the verb's unit and is not rule 18's added possessive. Likewise גָּוַע → 'give up the ghost' (13.19) keeps 'the' inside.

A preposition fused with מָה into one English interrogative — עַל־מָה and לָמָּה → 'Wherefore' (13.14, 13.24), כַּמָּה → 'How many' (13.23) — is one aligned unit headed on מָה as the morpheme carrying the interrogative content (rule 23); the preposition as first-token syntactic head is the competing reading, named in each note. Where the fused pair is the clause's predicate the construction copula joins it (13.23 'How many are').

וְאוּלָם → 'But' (13.4): one English word for two morphemes, so 'But' goes to אוּלָם, whose own lexeme it writes, and the waw is unrepresented (rule 14's וְעַתָּה count); giving 'But' to the waw is the competing reading. Bare אוּלָם → 'Surely' (13.3) takes its word alone.

amended.text: **A verb the ASV renders as a light verb plus a complement heads on the complement, not on the light verb.** This is rule 31's test applied to a verb: drop each word in turn, and the head is the one whose loss loses the lexeme. `הַאֲזִין` → *Give ear unto* heads on *ear*, because *give* alone gives anything; so too `הִשְׁתַּחֲוָה` → *did obeisance*, `נוֹעַץ` → *took counsel*, `הִמְלִיךְ` → *make king*, `הוֹדָה` → *give thanks*, `כִּלָּה` → *made an end*, `עוּד` → *bear witness*, `חָנַן` → *make supplication*, `בּוֹשׁ` → *put to shame*. The complement need not be a noun: an adjective (`הִכְבִּיד` → *made heavy*, `גָּדַל` → *make greater*) and a second verb (`חָטָא` hiphil → *made to sin*, `אָכַל` → *did eat*) are read the same way. Rule 24's *lexical predicate over subjects and auxiliaries* is about `was gathered`, and must not be read as a preference for the English verb — that reasoning would head *make king* on *make*. **A determiner or possessive the English idiom writes on such a complement is part of that one rendering.** Where the complement carries the source verb's lexeme and English writes it with an article or a possessive the idiom requires — `הֶחֱרִישׁ` → *held his peace*, `כִּלָּה` → *made an end*, `גָּוַע` → *give up the ghost* — that word joins the verb's unit with the complement, is never `added`, and does not move the head, which stays on the complement. Rule 18's closing sentence does not reach it: what that sentence marks `added` is a possessive standing on a noun the Hebrew writes with no suffix, or on a supplied object noun the sentences below leave `added` — `הָלַךְ` → *go* ***your way*** — and a possessive inside a complement that is itself the verb's rendering is neither. Test by subtraction as rule 31 does: drop the complement and the possessive has nothing to stand on, so the two go together, whereas dropping *your way* leaves *go* whole. The corpus reads `חָרֵשׁ` hiphil as *hold thy peace*, *held his peace*, *held their peace* and *hold my peace* in one unit headed on *peace* throughout its forty-two units and marks the possessive `added` in none. **A phrasal particle is not a complement.** `שָׁלַח` → *put forth*, `סוּר` → *take away*, and `נָתַן` → *put away* are one lexical verb plus its particle, and the head stays on the verb; the same subtraction says so, since *forth* and *away* alone name nothing. **But run that same subtraction on the particle before folding it in.** Where the bare English verb already writes the source verb's whole lexeme **and** the particle adds a direction, a result or a repetition the Hebrew does not write, no morpheme licenses that word: it is its own `added` unit under rule 30 and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside its rendering, exactly as this rule leaves a supplied object noun `added` and rule 17 a supplied lexical subject noun. `שׁוּב` → *turn ... again* keeps its *again* with the verb, discontinuous under rule 25, because *turn* alone does not write the returning, and `כָּנַס` → *gather ... together* and `מָצָא` → *find out* keep theirs on the same ground; but `בּוֹא` hiphil → *bring him* ***back*** leaves the *back* `added`, because the hiphil is the bringing and *bring* has already written it. **Both conditions must hold, and the second is read against the whole Hebrew clause and not against the verb alone.** What marks a particle surplus is that it states something the Hebrew has nowhere written, as the return of *bring him back* is: the particles this rule keeps — *out*, *together*, *away*, *forth* — stand beside verbs whose bare English word writes the lexeme quite as plainly as *bring* writes the bringing, so the first condition cannot decide a particle by itself. Where the direction the particle states is written in the clause by a preposition, an adverb or another morpheme, the particle restates what the Hebrew has written rather than supplying what it has not, and it is part of the English phrasal verb by which the ASV renders that verb: it joins the verb's unit, discontinuous around an object under rule 25, and the head is unaffected. `הָלַךְ` with `מִן` → *went* ***away*** *from him* and `לָקַח` with `עַל` → *took her* ***up*** *upon the ass* both keep their particle with the verb, on the same footing as `מָצָא` → *find out*. That the other morpheme holds an English word of its own is not a reason to mark the particle `added`, and it is not an invitation to move the particle onto that morpheme either: the word belongs to the verb's rendering, and a preposition already holding its own English is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw. Read the source verb's lexeme against the bare English verb rather than the shape of the English verb phrase, since the particle of *put forth* and *take away* is what completes a lexeme neither *put* nor *take* writes, and do not fold a surplus particle into the verb, the object or a preposition standing beside it, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and* and rule 51 about a supplied *also*. An ASV italic on such a particle corroborates it and decides nothing, by rule 7. **A supplied object is not a complement either, and that holds of any verb's rendering and not only a light verb's.** Where the ASV writes an object pronoun inside or beside a Hebrew verb's rendering — `וַיַּפֵּל` → *he let* ***it*** *fall*, `וַיַּשְׁקְ` → *gave* ***them*** *drink*, `אֲנִי שָׁמָעְתִּי` → *I have heard* ***it*** — read whether an object morpheme is present. Where one is, it takes the pronoun under rule 18 and the verb keeps the rest, as in `וַיַּעֲבִירֵם` → *caused* ***them*** *to pass through*. Where none is, the pronoun answers to no morpheme, is its own `added` unit under rule 30, and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside or beside its rendering; rule 17's permission reaches a pronoun realizing the verb's own person and number, and never an object the Hebrew does not write, exactly as that rule leaves a supplied lexical subject noun `added`. The verb's unit is discontinuous around such a pronoun under rule 25. **This applies only to a pronoun that truly supplies an object.** A reflexive pronoun the ASV uses to render the Hebrew verb's own voice or its elative sense is part of that verb's unit, because the source verb licenses it: `אִכַּף` → *bow myself* keeps *myself* with the Niphal verb and heads on *bow*, and `הִגְדִּיל עַל` → *magnified yourselves against* keeps *yourselves* with the Hiphil on the same ground. Position inside the English verb phrase is not what makes a word part of the verb's rendering — the complement, or the source verb's own voice or sense, must license it, and an unsupported object does not. **And a pronoun realizing the source verb's own person and number is not a supplied object either, whatever case the English recasting puts it in.** Where the ASV recasts a finite verb impersonally — writing a dummy or anticipatory *it* as the English subject and demoting the verb's own subject to the English object — both words belong to that verb's unit, headed on the lexical verb, exactly as rule 17 keeps a presentative dummy with the finite verb it recasts and rule 21 keeps *it was* with `הָיָה`: `נִלְאָה לַהֲשִׁיבָהּ אֶל־פִּיו` → ***It wearieth him*** *to bring it again to his mouth* gives *It wearieth him* to `נִלְאָה`, while the infinitive and the preposition keep their own English. What the preceding sentences govern is a pronoun denoting a participant the Hebrew never wrote, as the *it* of `וַיַּפֵּל` → *he let it fall* and the *them* of `וַיַּשְׁקְ` → *gave them drink* are; a pronoun denoting the very participant the verb's own person and number denote is not that, and marking it `added` would leave the verb's subject unrendered against rule 2 while an English word plainly realizing it stood unaligned. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the English pronoun and ask whether a participant the Hebrew wrote has lost its rendering, or only one the ASV supplied. Read whom the pronoun denotes rather than the case English puts it in, and read the Hebrew clause before reaching for this sentence: where an object morpheme stands in the clause it takes the pronoun under rule 18 as before, where the ASV writes the verb's subject as an English subject this sentence does not arise, and rule 20's ruling that a cleft or impersonal *it* is `added` governs a verbless clause, where no verb stands to be recast. **A supplied object noun is read on those same terms, and what decides it is whether the English noun writes the verb's own lexeme.** Where the ASV completes a Hebrew verb with an object noun the Hebrew does not write, run rule 31's subtraction on that noun. Where it does not carry the verb's lexeme, it answers to no morpheme, is its own `added` unit under rule 30, and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside its rendering: `לֹא שָׁאָלוּ` → *asked* ***counsel*** *not* leaves *counsel* `added`, because `שָׁאַל` is the asking and *asked* has already written it, and `הָלַךְ` → *go* ***your way*** leaves the supplied noun and its possessive `added` on the same ground, because *go* has written the going and *way* names a path the Hebrew does not write, exactly as rule 17 leaves a supplied lexical subject noun `added` and rule 20 a supplied lexical verb. A supplied noun is not a particle, and the clause-level reading above does not reach it: what that reading keeps with the verb is a word stating a relation the clause writes, and a noun naming a thing the clause never names is not that. Where the noun does carry the lexeme, it is part of that verb's one rendering, joins its unit, and the head goes by the same subtraction to whichever word carries the lexeme: `וַיַּעֲשׂוּ` → *did work* is one unit on the verb, headed on *did*, because `עָשָׂה` is the doing and the working alike and neither English word is a complement the other lacks. Read the source verb's lexeme rather than the English phrase's shape, since this rule's light-verb clause governs where the supplied noun is what carries that lexeme — `נוֹעַץ` → *took counsel* heads on *counsel* — and this sentence governs where the verb's own English word has written it already. A supplied possessive standing on such a noun is disposed of by rule 18's closing sentence and is not made the verb's by the noun beside it. **But a preposition the ASV supplies to reach the verb's own object is part of that rendering.** Where the Hebrew writes a bare direct object — no object marker on it and no preposition of its own — and the English verb reaches that object through a preposition the ASV has written, the preposition belongs to the verb's unit and not to the object noun's: `חָמְסוּ תוֹרָתִי` → *have done violence* ***to*** *my law*, `תְּבַצְּעִי רֵעַיִךְ` → *hast greedily gained* ***of*** *thy neighbors*, `הֵקַלּוּ אָב וָאֵם` → *have set light* ***by*** *father and mother*, `אֲבַקֵּשׁ אִישׁ` → *sought* ***for*** *a man*, `טָחוּ תָּפֵל` → *have daubed ... with untempered mortar*. This is rule 16's reasoning where no marker stands to take the word: the same subtraction test finds that dropping it diminishes nothing but the object relation, and the object noun's own English is the noun. The unit is discontinuous under rule 25 where other material stands between the verb and the preposition, and the head is unaffected — it stays on the lexical verb, or on the complement where this rule's light-verb clause puts it. **And the object so reached may be a pronominal suffix on the verb rather than a noun.** Where a verbal object suffix stands with no preposition of its own and the English rendering reaches it through a supplied preposition — `יִבְּמָהּ` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *her*, `יַבְּמִי` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *me* — that preposition belongs to the verb's unit on exactly the terms just given, and the suffix keeps only the pronoun rule 18 writes for it. Do not read rule 18's *the English pronoun that realizes it* as reaching the preposition standing beside that pronoun: what that rule places is the pronoun, and a preposition the English verb's valency licenses is the verb's whether its object is a noun or a suffix. Rule 40 does not reach such a suffix either, since no preposition morpheme stands in the clause for the recasting to silence. Test by subtraction as before — drop the English preposition and ask whether anything but the object relation is diminished. Two limits. Where an object marker or a preposition of the object's own is present, that morpheme takes the word under rules 16 and 11, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does. And this does not touch rule 33: a function word supplied for an adverbial accusative is licensed by that noun's own case-function and stays with the noun, whereas a word supplied for a direct object is licensed by the English verb's valency, so read which the Hebrew noun is before placing it.
amended.why: Rule 18's closing sentence marks a supplied possessive with no suffix `added`, and rule 44 itself leaves the possessive of `הָלַךְ` → *go your way* `added` with its supplied object; nothing in the contract says that the possessive of *hold his peace* — a complement that is the verb's own rendering — stays inside the verb's unit. JOB.13 writes the idiom three times (13.5, 13.13, 13.19), and the corpus reads every one of חָרֵשׁ's 42 units as a single unit headed on *peace* with the possessive inside (*hold thy peace* ×7, *held his peace*, *hold his peace*, *holdeth his peace*, *held their peace*, *hold my peace*, etc.), marking none `added`. The amendment states the boundary between the two cases by the subtraction test the rule already runs.

report: Checked all 32 candidate lemmas. Nearly every bucket difference is licensed by the source or the ASV: לְ unrepresented in 13.5 (הָיָה present, rule 21) vs 'shall be' in 13.16 (verbless, rule 49); הַ 'the' vs unrepresented follows whether the ASV wrote one; אִם 'Will' (disjunctive question) vs 'If' (conditional); עַל/עִמָּד/כְּ take whatever word the ASV wrote; 13.27 waws 'also' and 'And' per rule 51.

One real split: three preposition+מָה fusions. עַל־מָה (13.14) and לָמָּה (13.24) → 'Wherefore' are aligned units headed on מָה as the content morpheme; כַּמָּה (13.23) → 'How many are' was noncompositional headed on the first token כְּ. Patched 13.23 to aligned, source head s002 מָה, edges unchanged.

Added units re-checked against the dump: 13.9 anticipatory 'it' (rule 25), 13.18 'my' with no suffix (rule 18), 13.19 'that' over a finite clause juxtaposed to written הוּא which already holds 'he' (rules 17/55), 13.28 first 'that' over יִבְלֶה (rule 55) while the second 'that' goes to the resumptive suffix of אֲכָלוֹ (rule 18). No verse folds these into a neighbour, so no hidden split.

BSB disagreements are all convention: 13.4 waw of וְאוּלָם (one word for two morphemes; 'But' writes אוּלָם's lexeme, competing reading named in the note), paragogic nuns (rule 32), datives recast as possessives and the resultative לְ (rules 40/21), and אֶת in 13.10 (rule 16). None is a genuine error.

13.13 מִמֶּנִּי → 'let ... alone' was left as the verse pass read it (the ASV's rendering of the מִן phrase rather than a supplied lexical verb); it is a single instance and the note states the reading.
Recorded four conventions and one amendment to rule 44 (idiom possessive inside a light-verb complement, corpus-backed by the 42 חָרֵשׁ units).
